standard.title: Two-way tables and categorical relationships
standard.description: construct two-way tables and discuss possible relationship between categorical variables
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can construct scatterplots and describe association in terms of strength, direction and linearity (AC9M10ST03). They have not yet used two-way tables specifically to investigate relationships between categorical variables — this extends bivariate analysis from numerical to categorical data.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students construct two-way tables from categorical data sets and discuss possible relationships between categorical variables using frequencies and proportions.

nodes.label: Constructing two-way tables
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can organise categorical bivariate data into a two-way table with correct row and column structure.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a data set with two categorical variables, construct a two-way frequency table with appropriate row and column labels and correct cell counts.
nodes.typical_width: Construct two-way tables from raw data for multiple context types (survey data, observational data, experimental data); calculate row totals, column totals and grand total; verify accuracy by checking that margins sum correctly.
wider: Investigate a litter survey context — collect data on two categorical variables (e.g. type of litter and day of week) and construct a two-way table, explaining what the row and column structure reveals
Explore how two-way frequency tables are used in medical research and public health to organise data from observational studies

response_modes.reason: Tally and tabulation errors (double-counting, miscounting) are common. Fluency with accurate data organisation needs practice before proportional analysis.

success_criteria: Student correctly constructs a two-way table with accurate cell counts and marginal totals
Student labels rows and columns to correctly identify which variable is in which dimension

nodes.label: Using proportions to identify patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can calculate row or column proportions (or percentages) from a two-way table and use them to identify patterns across categories.
nodes.minimum_width: Calculate row or column percentages for a given two-way table; identify one pattern suggested by comparing proportions across categories.
nodes.typical_width: Calculate and interpret row proportions and column proportions for a two-way table; explain why proportions are more informative than raw counts when row/column sizes differ; identify patterns and associations by comparing conditional distributions across categories.
wider: Investigate survey responses using five-point Likert scales across two categories of respondents (e.g. junior vs senior students); use proportions to compare response patterns and discuss what the comparison reveals
Explore how two-way tables connect to conditional probability — P(response | group) is the conditional distribution, linking statistics to the probability work in AC9M10P01

response_modes.reason: Deciding whether to use row or column proportions requires explicit reasoning about which variable is being conditioned on. Students frequently use the wrong conditional direction — a systematic process for deciding is needed.

success_criteria: Student calculates row or column proportions correctly for a given two-way table
Student explains why proportions are more useful than raw counts for comparing categories of different sizes
nodes.hinge_reason: Using the wrong conditional direction (row vs column proportions) in N2 produces a fundamentally incorrect reading of the two-way table — N3 discussion of possible relationships is invalidated if the proportional comparison is pointed the wrong way.

nodes.label: Discussing possible relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use proportional patterns in a two-way table to make a defensible claim about a possible relationship between two categorical variables, using appropriate hedging language.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a pattern in a two-way table's proportions and state whether it suggests a possible relationship between the two variables, using appropriate language ('suggests', 'appears to').
nodes.typical_width: Discuss possible relationships between categorical variables using proportional evidence from two-way tables; use hedging language ('possible relationship', 'the data suggests'); acknowledge alternative explanations; discuss what additional data would strengthen or weaken the inference.
wider: Conduct a school-based litter survey collecting two categorical variables; construct the two-way table, calculate proportions and write a report discussing whether the data suggests a relationship — acknowledging limitations
Analyse a published two-way table from a public health or social context; evaluate the strength of the claimed relationship and identify what the table cannot tell us

response_modes.reason: The rhetorical skill of making a defensible but appropriately hedged statistical claim varies across context — the language appropriate for a school litter survey is different from medical research. Multiple context types build appropriate calibration of claim strength.

Discussing relationships integrates table construction (node 1), proportion calculation (node 2), and statistical reasoning about evidence strength into the full analysis act. This is the endpoint of the descriptor.

success_criteria: Student makes a claim about a possible relationship supported by proportional evidence from the table
Student uses hedging language that correctly reflects the strength of the evidence
